title.en: Real numbers: fixed point and floating point

hook.en: Your calculator shows 6.02 × 10^23 in a tiny display. Computers do the same with binary: a few bits for the digits and a few for where the point goes.

objectives.en: Convert simple binary fractions to decimal and back
Write a binary number in normalised mantissa–exponent form
Explain the trade-off between range and precision

narration.en: Your calculator shows 6.02 × 10^23 in a tiny display. Computers do the same with binary: a few bits for the digits and a few for where the point goes.

body.en: Places after the binary point are worth 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 … So 101.11 = 4 + 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 5.75. To convert a decimal fraction to binary, multiply the fraction by 2 again and again; the integer parts, read top to bottom, are the bits after the point. Some decimal fractions (like 0.1) never end in binary, which is why computers store them only approximately.

body.en: In floating-point form a real number is stored as a signed mantissa and a signed exponent: value = mantissa × 2^exponent. In normalised form the mantissa starts 0.1… (for a positive number), so no bits are wasted on leading zeros. With a fixed number of bits, more exponent bits give a bigger range and more mantissa bits give more precision. Fixed-point form, by contrast, keeps the point at a fixed place: simple, but with a small range. Java's float (32 bits) and double (64 bits) follow the IEEE 754 standard.

points.en: Exponent bits → range; mantissa bits → precision

body.en: The exponent is just the number of places the binary point jumped: jumps to the left give a positive exponent, jumps to the right a negative one. 0.00101 = 0.101 × 2^−2.
